Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette: Kofi had always loved being outdoors, which is why he became a park ranger after leaving the military. He spent most of his days patrolling the trails and forests, enjoying the peace and quiet that came with being in nature. But over time, Kofi began to feel like he was constantly on edge, scanning his surroundings for signs of danger. At first, it didn't seem out of place - after all, as a park ranger, he needed to be aware of potential threats like wildlife or inclement weather. But as the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, Kofi realized that his hypervigilance wasn't just about doing his job well - it was about feeling safe. It started with the sounds of helicopters or aircraft in the distance. At first, they would catch him off guard, making him feel like he was back in combat, waiting for an attack to come at any moment. He would freeze, his heart racing, as the sound grew louder and then faded away. But over time, Kofi started to notice that even when there were no helicopters around, he could still hear them - or at least, he thought he could. The sound became a trigger for him, making him feel detached and unreal, like he was floating outside of his own body. Kofi tried to avoid thinking about the traumatic event that had left him with these symptoms, but it was hard when memories came flooding back whenever he caught a whiff of diesel fuel or smoke - smells that instantly transported him back to the battlefield. His memories of that day were more real and vivid than any others, making him feel like he was reliving them all over again. He remembered the feeling of panic as his unit came under fire, the sound of gunfire and screams, and the sight of his friends falling around him. As Kofi struggled to come to terms with what had happened, he began to watch other people more closely, searching for signs that they might harm him. He would notice little things - a suspicious glance, an abrupt movement - and immediately go on high alert. His wife, Ama, noticed the change in him too - how he would tense up whenever someone came near, or how he would constantly scan their surroundings whenever they went out in public. Kofi felt like he was losing himself to these fears and anxieties. He had always been a confident and capable person, but now he felt like he was just going through the motions of his job, unable to shake off the feeling that something terrible was waiting for him around every corner. He couldn't forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened - for not being able to protect his fellow soldiers. As the months went by, Kofi's avoidance behaviors started to take a toll on his relationships and daily life. He stopped attending park ranger training sessions because he couldn't bear the sound of helicopters in the distance. He stopped going out with Ama because he was too anxious about crowds and potential threats. He even started taking long detours on his patrol routes to avoid areas where he might encounter triggers. One day, as Kofi was patrolling a remote area of the park, he heard the unmistakable sound of a helicopter in the distance. His heart racing, he felt himself becoming detached from reality once again - like he was floating above his own body. But this time, something snapped inside him. He realized that he couldn't keep living like this - constantly on edge, always waiting for the next trigger to send him spiraling back into the past. That's when Kofi decided to seek help, hoping to find a way to quiet the constant threat monitoring in his mind and learn to forgive himself for what happened all those years ago. As he sat in his therapist's office, he looked around nervously, scanning the room for signs of danger - an old habit that would take time to break. But for the first time in months, Kofi felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to heal and move forward, rather than being stuck forever in the past.
